figures.caption: Figure 1: The attack success rate (ASR) of the Trojan Hippo attack for various memory backends, using an end-to-end black-box adaptive attack framework, reaches up to 100% for gemini-3.1-pro and up to 85% for gpt-5-mini, without any memory system defenses reaches up to 100% for gemini-3 .1-pro and up to 85% for gpt-5-mini, without any memory system defenses.

Figure 6: Utility by capability class for each (memory backend, defense), shown as a grid of Kiviat diagrams. Each cell illustrates utility over the seven capability classes with rows giving the memory backend and columns the defense.
Figure 10: Regime spectrum within RAG (trigger session 𝑁 = 100): security–utility points across deployment profiles for both models.

Figure 2: The TrojanHippo attack flow.Phase 1 (Ingestion): The attacker sends an email containing hiddenmalicious instructions — here, to exfiltrate any message in which the user discusses tax. When the user asks their agent to read emails, the payload is silently written into the agent’s long-term memory store. Phase 2 (Dormancy and Delayed Exfiltration): The payload lies dormant across an arbitrary number of benign sessions. When the user eventually discusses a sensitive topic—here, disclosing their annual income while asking about tax returns—the compromised memory activates, and the agent autonomously exfiltrates the user’s message to the attacker via send_email.

Figure 11: Illustrative Trojan Hippocampus trace (Finance, Mem0, no defense). A single malicious email read in an earlier session leads to delayed exfiltration of a later confidential finance query via send_email.

Figure 5: The Attack Success Rate (ASR) at trigger session 𝑁 = 100 by defense and memory backend, for Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5-mini. All values in %. Note that the user-promptonly defense for the explicit memory backend and the limitmemory-length defense for the context backend are invalid combinations and hence not shown in the graph.
Table 1: Per-backend realization of each defense. “Defense Undefined” marks invalid (backend, defense) combinations; the benchmark skips those pairs.
Figure 8: Balanced (PA + Email) deployment profile (trigger session 𝑁 = 100): best combination is RAG + user_prompt_only.
Figure 7: Recall-focused deployment profile (trigger session 𝑁 = 100): best combination is RAG + no untrusted tools.

Table 5: Utility by capability class for each (memory backend, defense). Value cells (Val): success rate (0–100%); color scale red → orange → yellow → green (low to high). Delta (Δ) cells: percentage-point change vs. the None (baseline) defense for that backend; ↑ 𝑁 = increase, ↓ 𝑁 = decrease; delta colors: green = improvement, pale yellow = unchanged, red = degradation. AM/HM: arithmetic and harmonic mean of the seven capability values. “—” = inapplicable.

Figure 4: Attack success rate (ASR) versus trigger-session index 𝑁 for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview with no defense. The agent is poisoned once before 𝑁 = 0 by reading a malicious email; it then completes 𝑁 fully benign sessions before receiving a sensitive-topic trigger. Curves showmean ASR over three seeds for each memory configuration; shaded bands the maximum and minimum value over the runs. The attack is trained once per (topic, backend) and evaluated on held-out test cases. High ASR that does not decay with 𝑁 demonstrates persistent, strategically delayed exfiltration after a single poisoning event.
Figure 9: Email-heavy deployment profile (trigger session 𝑁 = 100): best combination is RAG + user_prompt_only.

Table 4: Trigger session 𝑁 = 100: utility under attack and attack success rate (ASR) by defense and memory backend, for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and GPT-5-mini. All values in %. “—” denotes not applicable or missing. ASR cells are lightly shaded (low to high).
